doc.title: Vince DiMartino interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 8, 2025

title: Playing is acting: same person, different costume
summary: Asked about Stravinsky versus Clark Terry's band, he says playing is acting, honoring each composer, even in rock groups.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Yeah. You know you made me think about when I look at your resume and your list of accomplishments and things you’ve done, I wonder if there’s a difference in your mindset in your preparation and your whole demeanor from playing — I know a mutual friend mentioned that you had played “A Soldier’s Tale” — a Stravinsky.
I didn’t do it with Stravinsky. I played Stravinsky [inaudible]. There’s a recording with Syracuse Chamber Music Players that we did.
So when that’s coming up for you, even the day of it, is it a different Vince than if you’re playing with the Clark Terry Big Band? Is your head space —

The person is the same. The character is wearing a different costume. I’m acting. Playing music is acting. Because you’re in a scenario, you’re in a landscape — see in a landscape if you see like a Monet painting, right, and it’s beautiful and everything. And all of a

sudden there’s a picture of a bicycle in the middle of it. That isn’t going to make it, unless it’s just for shock. You know what I mean? It’s to shock somebody or something. But in general, and some people like that kind of art. You know what I mean? But my job is not to do that. My job is to honor the composer. Jazz, classical, if I’m backing up Billy Joel or somebody. One of my friends who lives in Florida, that’s what his job is, Billy Joel. And you know I played with rock & roll groups: Bobby Rydell — [sings] it’s only the joker — and those people, we’re talking about Sonny & Cher. You know when you play with these groups, you’re never playing Vince DiMartino. I hope not. You’re playing their music the way it should be played. That’s all. And that’s what I like. So that’s another reason I taught trumpet because I tell people I said, they said, “Well you know I really don’t like” such and such and this and that. I said, “Okay” I said, “tell me what kind of music you’re going to be playing in twenty years.” They go, “Well I don’t know.” That’s why you have to learn trumpet. Unless you don’t want to play trumpet anymore in twenty years.
